# Methods

## Overview of the simulation study

We designed the simulation study following the aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures structure recommended for simulation studies that evaluate statistical methods (DiRenzo et al., 2023; Williams et al., 2024). The study had three aims: (i) to estimate how the shape of the phylogenetic tree, measured as the distribution of branching times (the γ statistic; Pybus & Harvey, 2000) and the imbalance of the topology (the Colless index; Colless, 1982), affects the type I error and the power of tests that relate the phylogenetic structure of metacommunities to an environmental gradient; (ii) to estimate how the same tests perform under different processes of metacommunity assembly, which, to the best of our knowledge, neither the articles that proposed these tests nor later evaluations of them have addressed (Peres-Neto & Kembel, 2015; Duarte et al., 2016); and (iii) to estimate how well ordination and factorization methods recover a clade associated with the gradient. We generated metacommunities in two layers (Fig. 1). Layer A follows the static protocol of Peres-Neto, Leibold and Dray (2012), which was also used to validate the tests we evaluated, so our results can be compared directly with the published ones. Layer B simulates metacommunity dynamics with the process-based framework of Thompson et al. (2020), in which species sorting, mass effects and competition emerge from local population dynamics and dispersal.

We stated four hypotheses before the main runs. We expected that (i) tree imbalance would move the type I error of the taxa shuffle away from the nominal level, since the phylogenetic weights of matrix P are heterogeneous among tips in imbalanced trees (H1); (ii) phylogenetic signal in niche breadth or maximum abundance would inflate the type I error of all tests, with a magnitude that depends on tree shape (H2); (iii) very negative γ, that is, long internal branches near the root, would concentrate variation on the first PCPS axis and favour the recovery of basal over recent clades (H3); and (iv) the ranking of the methods in power and in clade recovery would change with tree shape (H4). The study was not registered. However, we wrote the design and the hypotheses down before the main runs (docs/PLANO_SIMULACAO.md, first committed on 16 October 2026 as commit 668fa60 of the code repository), and we report the departures from that plan where they occur.

![Schematic of the simulation design. Notice that tree shape is controlled before traits are simulated, so that every trait scenario and every assembly process is crossed with the same grid of tree shapes, and that the inference step uses the same two permutation null models for all tests on matrix P.](figures/fig1_schematic.png){#fig-design width=100%}

## Tree generation and the tree-shape grid

We controlled γ and the Colless index independently by generating topology and branching times from separate processes. We drew topologies from Aldous's β-splitting model (Aldous, 1996), in which β = 0 gives Yule trees and smaller values give increasingly imbalanced trees, and branching times from a pure-birth process in which each of the k lineages diversifies at rate k^c, so that c = 0 corresponds to a Yule process and c < 0 to a slowdown in diversification, as under diversity dependence, which produces negative γ. We then ordered the nodes by a uniform linear extension of the partial order of the tree and set the root depth to one. Because γ depends only on the intervals between nodes and the Colless index only on the topology, this construction controls the two axes separately. This generator is our own design choice and not a published model; it replaced the library of trees from several generators, sampled by strata, that we had planned, because it gives independent control by construction.

We took the levels of the grid from the empirical distribution of tree shape in anurans. We pruned all clades with 40–250 tips from the time-calibrated species-level tree of Portik et al. (2023) and computed γ and the Colless index normalized against its Yule expectation with the R package treestats v. 1.71.13 (Janzen & Etienne, 2024). For each pool size N (50, 100 and 200 species, as in Duarte et al., 2016), γ took three levels, namely zero (as in a Yule tree), the median of the empirical clades and their 10% quantile, and the Colless index took three levels, zero, the median and the 90% quantile (Table S1). We calibrated c and β for each N with curves of the mean statistic against the parameter, and accepted a tree only when both statistics fell within 0.5 units of the targets of its cell, which gave acceptance rates of 9–25%. Thus, every cell of the 3 × 3 grid could be filled, and the grid spans the empirical range of anuran tree shapes between the 10% and 90% quantiles, although it has no level with γ > 0. The Yule × Yule cell approximates the trees used in previous validations (Peres-Neto & Kembel, 2015; Duarte et al., 2016), since the acceptance window truncates the Yule distribution of both statistics. We drew 1,000 trees per cell and N, and replicate r of every scenario used tree r of its cell, so that the scenarios were paired by tree.

## Layer A: static metacommunities

Each metacommunity had 100 sites along an environmental gradient E drawn from a uniform distribution between 0 and 100. The expected abundance of species j at site i followed a Gaussian response, L_ij = h_j exp[−(E_i − u_j)² / (2σ_j²)], and we drew the observed abundance from a Poisson distribution with mean L_ij (Peres-Neto et al., 2012). We simulated the optimum u_j as a continuous trait on the tree under Brownian motion transformed by Pagel's λ (Pagel, 1999) and rescaled it to the interval [−1, 101]; niche breadth σ_j came from a normal distribution with mean 10 and standard deviation 10, truncated at zero, and maximum abundance h_j from a uniform distribution between 0 and 30. In addition, σ_j and h_j could carry phylogenetic signal. In that case, we simulated a Brownian trait on the tree (λ = 1) and imposed on it the same marginal distribution by ranks, so that scenarios with and without signal differed only in how the values were arranged on the tree. We removed empty sites and pruned species absent from every site from the tree before analysis, as one would with real data, and analysed both incidence and abundance data.

## Layer B: process-based metacommunities

Layer B followed the equations of Thompson et al. (2020), which we implemented in R because neither the original Julia code nor the R package mcomsimr (Thompson et al., 2020) carries a licence. At each time step, the expected abundance of species j at site i was its density-independent growth rate, a Gaussian function of the mismatch between u_j and E_i with breadth σ_j and maximum r_j, multiplied by its abundance and divided by one plus the sum of the competitive effects of all species at the site, following a Beverton–Holt model (Beverton & Holt, 1957). We then drew abundances from a Poisson distribution; each individual emigrated with probability a, and each site received immigrants in proportion to the emigrants from all other sites. The environment was static and the sites had no spatial structure, because the dispersal kernel was uniform. This keeps sites exchangeable, so that the site shuffle remains a valid null model and spatial autocorrelation does not confound the phylogenetic tests. All species were seeded with Poisson(0.5) individuals per site every 10 steps during the first 100 steps, the dynamics ran for 1,000 steps, and we analysed the final state as incidence data. Maximum growth rate r_j, drawn from a uniform distribution between 2 and 8, took the role of h_j in the trait scenarios.

We crossed two dispersal regimes with two competition structures, giving four archetypes. Dispersal was low (a = 0.01) in species sorting and high (a = 0.5) in mass effects. Competition was either intraspecific only or also interspecific and structured by phylogeny: interspecific coefficients came from a uniform distribution between 0 and 0.1, relative to an intraspecific coefficient of 1 (both multiplied by 0.05), and were assigned to species pairs by the rank of their phylogenetic similarity, so that close relatives competed more strongly. Since competition and dispersal remove species, the cell of the grid defined the tree of the regional pool rather than the tree of the analysed metacommunity. We therefore calibrated the size of the pool for each archetype, scenario and N so that the mean number of species left after the dynamics was close to N, and drew the pool tree with the targets of its cell, recalibrating β and c for each pool size. However, mass effects with phylogenetic competition could not reach N = 200, since pools of up to 2,900 species left only about 150 species, and we dropped this combination. Layer B used five cells of the grid (the four corners and the centre) and 1,000 replicates per combination, and we recorded γ and the Colless index of both the pool tree and the analysed tree.

## Scenarios and estimands

The eight trait scenarios were the same in both layers (Table 1). In S0 and S1, we analysed a gradient independent of the one that generated the data, with species optima without (S0) or with (S1) phylogenetic signal, so any association between phylogenetic structure and the analysed gradient arises by chance. Scenarios S2, S2σ and S2h used the gradient that generated the data with optima without phylogenetic signal, so they estimate the type I error of the phylogenetic component of each test. S2σ and S2h add phylogenetic signal in niche breadth or in maximum abundance, which creates a nuisance structure, that is, a phylogenetic pattern in the data that is not an association between phylogeny and the gradient. The scenarios under the alternative hypothesis had optima with intermediate (S3a, λ = 0.5) or full (S3b, λ = 1) phylogenetic signal, and S3σ added signal in niche breadth. Accordingly, the estimand of every test was its rejection rate at α = 0.05, which is the type I error in S0–S2h and the power in S3a–S3σ. For aim (iii), the estimand was the probability that a method identifies a planted clade.

| Scenario | Optima (λ) | Signal in σ or h | Gradient analysed | Estimand |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S0 | 0 | none | independent | type I error |
| S1 | 1 | none | independent | type I error |
| S2 | 0 | none | generating | type I error (phylogenetic component) |
| S2σ | 0 | σ | generating | type I error under nuisance structure |
| S2h | 0 | h | generating | type I error under nuisance structure |
| S3a | 0.5 | none | generating | power |
| S3b | 1 | none | generating | power |
| S3σ | 1 | σ | generating | power under nuisance structure |

: Trait scenarios of both layers. λ is Pagel's λ of the species optima. {#tbl-scenarios}

## Methods compared

All tests relate the matrix P of phylogeny-weighted species composition (Pillar & Duarte, 2010; Duarte et al., 2016), or the phylogenetic eigenvectors, to the gradient. We computed P with phylogenetic fuzzy weighting and the square-rooted Bray–Curtis dissimilarity between sites (D_P), and tested its association with E with a permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA; Anderson, 2001) and a Mantel test (Mantel, 1967), as in Duarte et al. (2016). We also extracted the principal coordinates of phylogenetic structure (PCPS; Duarte, 2011; Duarte et al., 2012) from D_P and fitted a linear model of each of the first two axes on E (GLM PCPS1 and GLM PCPS2); in Layer B, we also fitted a redundancy analysis of both axes on E (RDA PCPS). We re-implemented the phylogenetic community composition approach (PCC) of Peres-Neto and Kembel (2015) from the equations in the original article, using the variance of the adjusted R² across phylogenetic eigenvectors as the test statistic. Every test was evaluated with 999 permutations under two null models, the site shuffle, which permutes the sites, and the taxa shuffle, which permutes the tips of the tree while keeping its topology. We report the largest of the two P-values (max test), which controls the type I error when either null hypothesis holds (Peres-Neto & Kembel, 2015; Duarte et al., 2016). We wrote the permutation loops ourselves for efficiency and checked, in unit tests, that the observed statistics equal those of the R packages vegan v. 2.7-6 (Oksanen et al., 2026) and PCPS v. 1.0.9 (Debastiani, 2026).

## Recovery of a planted clade

To evaluate aim (iii), we planted a clade associated with the gradient in each replicate of Layer A. We drew one internal node whose clade held 10–30% of the tips, either among the older or among the younger half of the eligible nodes, so that basal and recent clades of similar size could be compared. The optima of all species were u_j = −1 + 102 Φ(z_j + δI_j), where z_j are independent standard normal deviates, I_j indicates membership of the planted clade and δ is the shift; the other species therefore had no phylogenetic signal in their optima, and the shift has the same meaning for every tree size. We used shifts of 0.5, 1 and 2, all nine cells of the grid, N = 50, 100 and 200 with incidence data, and N = 100 with abundance data, with 1,000 replicates per combination. For a given replicate, the planted clade, the optima and the gradient were the same across shifts and data types, so that only the factor of interest changed. This objective replaced the per-node effect sizes under continuous Brownian motion that we had planned, because a planted clade defines unambiguously which answer is correct.

We compared four methods. For PCPS, PCC and the evolutionary principal component analysis (evoPCA; Pavoine, 2016), each method took the axis most correlated with E among its first four, and the score of each internal node was the absolute correlation between membership of its clade and the species scores on that axis. The species scores were the correlations of the columns of P with the PCPS axis, which equal the species scores of the R package PCPS; the values of the phylogenetic eigenvector; and the correlations of the species columns of the Hellinger-transformed table of evoPCA (Legendre & Gallagher, 2001), computed with the R package adiv v. 2.2.1 (Pavoine, 2020). We did not use the branch loadings of evoPCA because, with incidence data, a branch is present wherever any of its descendants is, so the branch above a planted clade saturates and small subclades always correlate better with the axis. For phylofactorization (Washburne et al., 2017), the score of each split was the objective of the algorithm, the deviance explained by the phylogenetic factor in a binomial model with incidence data or the variance explained by the isometric log-ratio balance with abundance data; we computed it for every node, which gives the same best split as the R package phylofactor v. 0.0.1 (Washburne et al., 2017) while also ranking all nodes. A method recovered the clade when its best-scoring clade was the planted one or its complement. As complementary measures, which give partial credit to a method that chooses a nested or a slightly larger clade, we recorded the rank of the planted node among all nodes and the Jaccard similarity between the best-scoring and the planted clades.

## Performance measures and Monte Carlo error

The performance measure of each test was its rejection rate across the 1,000 replicates of a condition, and that of each clade-recovery method was its proportion of hits. With K = 1,000 replicates, the Monte Carlo standard error of a rate p is [p(1 − p)/K]^½, which is 0.007 at P = 0.05 and at most 0.016 at P = 0.5, so a 95% Monte Carlo interval around the nominal level spans about ±0.014. We chose K so that this interval falls within Bradley's liberal criterion for acceptable type I error, [0.025, 0.075] (Bradley, 1978), and used 999 permutations so that P-values have a resolution of 0.001. We report every rate with its Monte Carlo standard error in the Supporting Information (Table S2), and the credible intervals of the formal models below include the binomial variation among replicates.

## Statistical models of the simulation results

We modelled the rates aggregated by condition with beta-binomial models fitted in the R package brms v. 2.23.0 (Bürkner, 2017) with CmdStan v. 2.39.0 through cmdstanr v. 0.9.0 (Gabry et al., 2025), with one model for the type I error and one for the power in each layer, and one for clade recovery. The plan was to treat γ and the Colless index as continuous covariates, but each cell of the grid has a single target per axis, and Layer A did not store the shape of every tree, so a continuous term would only interpolate three points. Therefore, we entered the levels of γ and of the Colless index as factors, with their interaction, which estimates the full γ × imbalance surface without assuming its form. In Layer A, the shape effects could differ among tests and scenarios, which is what testing a nuisance effect that depends on tree shape requires, and with N and data type; in the R formula notation, the model was test * scenario * (γ + Colless) + test * (γ:Colless + N + data type) + test:(γ + Colless):(N + data type) + test:scenario:N, where the last term lets the scenario effects, such as the inflation under nuisance structure, differ with N. In Layer B, where only five cells were simulated, the cell entered as a five-level factor, in test * archetype * (scenario + cell) + test * N * (archetype + scenario + cell). The clade-recovery model was method * (γ * depth + Colless + γ:Colless + shift + N + data type) + method:(γ + Colless):(N + data type + shift). We first fitted quasibinomial generalized linear models to the same structures, which showed a dispersion 2.1–8.5 times larger than binomial. The beta-binomial accounts for this extra variation with a single precision parameter φ, whereas a first version with an observation-level random effect hit the maximum tree depth of the sampler in almost every transition.

Priors were declared explicitly on the logit scale. We used normal(0, 1.5) for all coefficients; normal(−2.9, 1.5) for the intercept of the type I models, centred on logit(0.05), and normal(0, 1.5) for the other intercepts; and gamma(2, 0.01) for φ, which is weakly informative around the values implied by the quasibinomial dispersion (φ of about 130–910). We ran four chains of 2,000 iterations (1,000 of warm-up) with adapt_delta = 0.95 and a maximum tree depth of 12, since with the default of 10 a few transitions of the type I models reached the limit. We checked convergence with the rank-normalized R̂, the bulk and tail effective sample sizes, the number of divergent transitions and the number of transitions at the maximum tree depth, and model fit with in-sample posterior predictive checks, both for each condition and for the sums over the conditions of each test, N and cell. We summarize the results as posterior rates and contrasts between tree shapes or archetypes, with medians and 95% credible intervals (CI). Because the raw rates can still exceed the modelled ones in the most extreme conditions, we also report them where they do.

## Empirical reference and case study

To show where real regional species pools fall in the grid of tree shapes, and how the methods behave with real data, we used 14 tadpole metacommunities compiled from the literature and from unpublished data (Box 1). We harmonized species names with the Amphibian Species of the World (Frost, 2026; through the internal dataset of AmphiNom, updated on 16 October 2025) using the R package AmphiNom v. 1.1.0 (Liedtke, 2019), excluded undetermined taxa, and matched the remaining 123 species to the tips of the Portik et al. (2023) tree. We built three nested pools (Atlantic Forest; Atlantic Forest and interior of São Paulo; all South American metacommunities), pruned the tree to each, and computed γ and the normalized Colless index on the point-estimate tree and on its 100 time-calibrated bootstrap trees. For the case study, we used the metacommunities with at least 10 ponds and pond depth measured in every pond, namely two of the 14 and one additional published dataset: Serra da Bocaina (13 ponds; Provete et al., 2014), southern Brazil (32 ponds; Both et al., 2011) and northwestern São Paulo (40 ponds; Prado & Rossa-Feres, 2014). We applied all tests and the four clade-scoring methods to incidence data with pond depth as the gradient, and also with canopy cover in Bocaina, the variable associated with its phylogenetic composition in a previous analysis with PCPS (Provete, 2018).

## Implementation and reproducibility

We ran all analyses in R v. 4.6.1 (R Core Team, 2026), with the versions of every package recorded in the lockfile of renv v. 1.3.1 (Ushey & Wickham, 2026); trees were handled with ape v. 5.8-1 (Paradis & Schliep, 2019), and the trait simulation, the β-splitting and branching-time generator and the calibration of the grid are our own R code in the repository. We orchestrated the simulations of Layer A and Layer B with targets v. 1.12.0 (Landau, 2021) and crew v. 1.3.3 (Landau, 2026) in a Docker image on spot cloud instances with 192 virtual CPUs (190 workers); the pipeline seed was 20261018, from which targets derives one seed per branch. Layer A took about 8 h for the 432,000 metacommunities of the main run and Layer B about 7.5 h for its 440,000. The clade-recovery runs took 1.2 h on a 16-core workstation, with one seed per tree, depth and replicate, and each formal model 1–7 min. Code is available at [CITAR: GitHub repository and Zenodo DOI], together with the rates aggregated by condition and the scripts that compute the performance measures and the models from them, which reproduce every table and figure without rerunning the simulations.

# Results

## Validation

The static layer reproduced the published validations. In the Yule trees of Duarte et al. (2016), the rejection rates of the site shuffle, the taxa shuffle and the max test fell within the 95% binomial interval of our estimates in 66 of 72 cells. The six exceptions came from four conditions (PERMANOVA with both components at N = 100, with environment only at N = 200 and with phylogeny only at N = 200, and the Mantel test with environment only at N = 200), slightly more than the 3.6 cells expected by chance. The mean PERMANOVA R² and Mantel ρ agreed to the second decimal place when we used the Bray–Curtis dissimilarity without the square root, as in the code of Duarte et al. (2016); in the rest of the study we used the square-rooted version. The PCC matched the published rates in the scenarios that do not depend on the tree. Its power was lower than published (0.93 against 0.95), and it varied between 0.71 and 0.93 among 20 Yule trees, so the published values lie just above that range, which seems to reflect a single favourable tree. Thus, our implementation closely reproduces both benchmarks.

## Type I error under tree shape and nuisance structure

Tree imbalance did not affect the type I error of any test. In all 75 combinations of test, null scenario and N, the difference in the distance of the type I error from the nominal level between highly imbalanced and Yule trees was within ±0.012, and no 95% CI excluded zero, with incidence or abundance data (@fig-type1). In S0, where optima had no phylogenetic signal and the gradient was independent, all tests were conservative, and four of them became more conservative in trees with low γ (by 0.008–0.020). Therefore, H1 was not supported at the resolution of our design, although we did not test the medium level of imbalance separately from the high one.

Phylogenetic signal in niche breadth inflated the type I error of only two tests. Compared with the same scenario without signal (S2), signal in σ (S2σ) increased the rejection rate of GLM PCPS2 by 0.02 (95% CI 0.01–0.03) in Yule trees at N = 100, and by 0.05 (0.04–0.06), 0.10 (0.08–0.12) and 0.21 (0.19–0.23) with low γ at N = 50, 100 and 200 (@fig-type1). The raw rates reached 0.36 at N = 200 in low-γ trees. The PCC was also inflated, by 0.05 (0.03–0.06) in Yule trees and by 0.02 (0.01–0.03) with low γ at N = 100, with raw rates of up to 0.22 at N = 200 in Yule trees. Interestingly, PERMANOVA, GLM PCPS1 and the Mantel test became more conservative under signal in σ (by 0.005–0.030), and signal in maximum abundance (S2h) did not change the rejection rate of any test. With abundance data, the inflation of GLM PCPS2 was smaller (0.08, 0.06–0.09, with low γ at N = 100). As a result, H2 was rejected as stated: the nuisance structure created by a phylogenetically conserved niche breadth seems to affect only the methods that rely on the second PCPS axis or on phylogenetic eigenvectors, and its effect on GLM PCPS2 depends strongly on the distribution of branching times.

![Type I error of each test over the γ × Colless grid at N = 100 with incidence data (posterior medians of the beta-binomial model). Notice that rows S0 to S2h are almost uniform across the grid, whereas GLM PCPS2 doubles its rejection rate in the low-γ cells of S2σ.](figures/fig2_type1.png){#fig-type1 width=100%}

## Power and tree shape

The distribution of branching times, but not imbalance, changed the power of most tests (@fig-power). At N = 100 with incidence data, low γ reduced the power of GLM PCPS1 from 0.74 to 0.34 in S3b (contrast −0.40, 95% CI −0.45 to −0.34), with similar losses in S3a and S3σ, and that of the PCC from 0.98 to 0.73 (−0.25, −0.30 to −0.21). The Mantel test lost 0.05–0.14 at N = 100 and up to 0.23 at N = 50. In contrast, the power of PERMANOVA did not change with γ at N = 100 in S3b (0.01, −0.02 to 0.05), was lower with low γ at N = 50 (−0.03 to −0.17 across scenarios) and higher at N = 200 (+0.04 to +0.08). High imbalance reduced power by at most 0.09. Consequently, the ranking of the tests changed with tree shape: in S3b, the PCC was the most powerful test in Yule trees and the third with low γ, and in S3a GLM PCPS1 fell from third to fourth. The effect of γ also changed with N in opposite directions among tests, since the loss of GLM PCPS1 increased with N (−0.38 at N = 50 and −0.46 at N = 200 in S3b), whereas that of the PCC decreased (−0.48 at N = 50 and −0.06 at N = 200). Thus, H4 was supported for power.

![Power of each test over the γ × Colless grid at N = 100 with incidence data (posterior medians). Notice that the low-γ rows lose power in GLM PCPS1 and PCC, whereas PERMANOVA keeps a similar power in every cell.](figures/fig3_power.png){#fig-power width=100%}

## Performance under metacommunity assembly processes

The assembly process mattered more than tree shape for power (@fig-layerB). Under species sorting without competition, power at N = 100 in S3b in Yule pool trees ranged from 0.78 (GLM PCPS1) and 0.83 (RDA PCPS) to 0.87 (PERMANOVA), 0.92 (Mantel) and 0.96 (PCC), whereas GLM PCPS2 had almost no power (0.03), as in Layer A. Mass effects reduced the power of every test except GLM PCPS2, which gained 0.08 (0.06–0.11) from its low baseline. Relative to species sorting, PERMANOVA lost 0.62 (0.58–0.65) in Yule pool trees and 0.72 (0.69–0.75) with low γ, the Mantel test 0.75 and 0.79, RDA PCPS 0.58 and 0.55, GLM PCPS1 0.55 and 0.27, and the PCC 0.93 (0.92–0.94) and 0.76, so that the PCC detected the phylogenetic signal in almost no replicates. Surprisingly, adding phylogenetic competition to mass effects partly restored the power of every test except the PCC; for instance, PERMANOVA lost 0.46 (0.42–0.50) instead of 0.62 in Yule pool trees. Under species sorting, phylogenetic competition changed power by −0.12 to +0.11. These two contrasts should be read with care, because competition prunes close relatives and changes the shape of the analysed tree relative to the pool tree, so the effect of the process cannot be separated from that of a change in tree shape; this pruning is strongest under mass effects, where the Colless index of the analysed tree was about 75% lower than that of the pool. Under the null hypothesis, no lower CI bound exceeded 0.075 at N = 100 (largest posterior median 0.088). However, raw rejection rates exceeded that limit for GLM PCPS2 in S2σ under species sorting (0.094 at N = 100 and 0.104–0.129 at N = 200 in the low- and mid-γ cells) and for the PCC in S2h (0.085–0.089 at N = 100; 0.111 under species sorting and 0.116–0.143 under mass effects at N = 200).

![Power in Layer B by assembly archetype and pool tree cell at N = 100 (posterior medians and 95% credible intervals). Notice that mass effects (orange) lower the power of every test except GLM PCPS2 and almost abolish that of the PCC, and that phylogenetic competition under mass effects (pink) recovers part of the power lost.](figures/fig4_layerB_power.png){#fig-layerB width=100%}

## Recovery of a planted clade

The evoPCA and phylofactorization recovered the planted clade far more often than PCPS and PCC (@fig-clade). With a shift of 2 and incidence data, evoPCA and phylofactorization identified the planted node in 0.44–0.88 of the replicates, depending on N and depth, and recovered basal clades more often than recent ones (0.79 against 0.66 at N = 100). PCPS recovered the clade in 0.12–0.42 of the replicates and PCC in only 0.08–0.12. The complementary measures agree with this ranking: at N = 100, the median rank of the planted node was 1 for evoPCA and phylofactorization, 2 (basal clades) and 6 (recent clades) for PCPS, and 7 and 9 for PCC, and the mean Jaccard similarity between the chosen and the planted clades was 0.89–0.94, 0.60–0.75 and 0.45–0.50, respectively. Hence, PCPS often chose a clade that overlapped the planted one, whereas PCC usually chose a different part of the tree, which seems to reflect that its four leading eigenvectors follow the deepest splits. With a shift of 0.5, no method exceeded 0.21.

Tree shape changed recovery only for PCPS and PCC. With low γ, PCPS recovered basal clades in 0.58 of the replicates against 0.21 in Yule trees, and recent clades in 0.35 against 0.04 (N = 100), and this advantage grew with N (+0.23 to +0.45 across N and depths). The PCC lost 0.10–0.14 in basal clades with low γ and gained 0.07–0.09 in recent ones, whereas the recovery of evoPCA and phylofactorization did not change with γ (all 95% CI included zero), and high imbalance reduced recovery by 0.01–0.10 in all methods. Interestingly, low γ improved PCPS for recent as well as for basal clades, so H3 was only partly supported: the advantage of basal clades seems to be a matter of degree rather than a different behaviour of the method, and the share of variation on the first PCPS axis decreased rather than increased with low γ in the descriptive summaries of Layer A. With abundance data, the patterns were the same, with lower recovery for the compositional phylofactorization (0.68 and 0.56 for basal and recent clades at N = 100) than for evoPCA (0.78 and 0.65), and PCPS gained 0.29 (0.25–0.33) and 0.23 (0.21–0.25) with low γ. Taken together, H4 was also supported for clade recovery, but only through the change in rank between PCPS and PCC.

![Probability of recovering the planted clade over the γ × Colless grid at N = 100, incidence data and a shift of 2 (posterior medians), for basal (old) and recent (young) clades. Notice that PCPS gains markedly with low γ and PCC changes in opposite directions for basal and recent clades, whereas evoPCA and phylofactorization recover the clade at a similar rate in every cell.](figures/fig5_clade.png){#fig-clade width=100%}

## Convergence and fit of the formal models

All models converged, with R̂ ≤ 1.01, bulk effective sample size ≥ 908 and tail effective sample size ≥ 1,477, no divergent transitions and no transition at the maximum tree depth (Table S3). The in-sample 95% posterior predictive intervals contained 96–98% of the observed rates of each condition and the 50% intervals 61–70%, so the predictive intervals are slightly wider than needed; when we summed the conditions of each test, N and cell, every group fell within its 95% interval.

# Box 1. Real pools and real metacommunities

The three regional pools of anurans fell inside the grid of tree shapes (@fig-box1). The Atlantic Forest pool (60 species) had γ = −2.51 and a normalized Colless index of 0.67; adding the metacommunities of the interior of São Paulo (81 species) lowered γ to −3.16 with the same Colless index (0.67), and the South American pool (123 species) had γ = −3.90 and a Colless index of 1.99. Thus, γ of the three pools lies between the Yule and the median levels of the grid, and imbalance between the Yule and the median levels except in the largest pool, which lies between the median and the 90% quantile. Across the 100 bootstrap trees of Portik et al. (2023), γ varied by about one unit and the Colless index by up to 1.1 units, and the point-estimate tree sat at the lower edge of the distribution of γ, probably because the bootstrap trees differ in topology and have deeper roots. As a consequence, the low-γ cells, where we found the largest effects of tree shape, are more extreme than these pools, but within the range of the anuran clades used to define the grid.

The three metacommunities of the case study had small trees with contrasting shapes. Bocaina (Provete et al., 2014; 15 species in 13 ponds) and southern Brazil (Both et al., 2011; 21 species in 32 ponds) had negative γ (−1.59 and −1.53), whereas northwestern São Paulo (Prado & Rossa-Feres, 2014; 26 species in 40 ponds) had positive γ (1.39), outside the range of the grid. No test rejected the null hypothesis of no association between phylogenetic structure and pond depth with the max test (all P ≥ 0.107). In Bocaina, canopy cover was marginally associated with phylogenetic composition under the site shuffle (P = 0.048 for PERMANOVA and 0.050–0.053 for GLM PCPS1, RDA PCPS and PCC), but not under the taxa shuffle (P = 0.23–0.56). This seems to indicate that canopy cover is related to the composition of these ponds, in line with the analysis with PCPS of Provete (2018), but that the phylogenetic arrangement of the species adds no detectable signal once the tips are permuted, which is the inference the max test protects. The clade-scoring methods partly agreed: in Bocaina, PCC, evoPCA and phylofactorization chose the same clade of five Dendropsophus and Scinax species along the depth gradient, and in northwestern São Paulo PCC and evoPCA chose the three microhylids; the agreement of the PCC is unexpected, given its poor recovery in the simulations. However, with 13–40 ponds and without a significant test, these clades describe the strongest phylogenetic contrast along the gradient rather than a demonstrated association.

![Tree shape of three nested regional pools of anurans (coloured points, point-estimate tree; bars, 2.5–97.5% quantiles across 100 bootstrap trees, centred on their median) against the targets of the simulation grid (open symbols, by N) and the anuran clades with 40–250 tips of Portik et al. (2023) (grey points). Notice that the pools fall inside the grid and close to its Yule and median levels.](figures/box1_pools.png){#fig-box1 width=85%}
